title: The Complicated Case of Passing On Your Digital Estate
gist: US digital-inheritance law (RUFADAA, enacted in 48 states plus DC and the US Virgin Islands) collides with the federal Stored Communications Act so that a named fiduciary can close a decedent's accounts but gets only metadata catalogs unless content access is explicitly granted in a will; meanwhile platform legacy tools from Google, Apple and Meta legally override those written instructions, there is no standard protocol to even notify a provider that a user died, and self-custodied crypto without a key is permanently lost.

insights.claim: The Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (RUFADAA) has been enacted in 48 US states plus Washington, DC and the US Virgin Islands, with Massachusetts having adopted but not yet enacted it and Louisiana passing a similar but different law of its own.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Digital-estate products can be built to a near-national single legal standard, but Louisiana and Massachusetts require carve-outs — a compliance cost line item for any estate-tech or custodial platform.

insights.claim: The binding constraint on releasing a dead person's online data is the federal Stored Communications Act, which bars companies holding online assets from releasing them without the user's permission — RUFADAA exists to grant survivors rights while preserving the original holder's privacy.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Platform refusal to hand over a decedent's data is a federal-liability posture, not customer-service obstruction — expect providers to stay maximally restrictive until the statute changes.
insights.quote: The real point of conflict, according to Orzeske, lies in the Stored Communications Act, a federal law that says companies that handle our online assets can't release them without our permission.

insights.claim: Under RUFADAA the default for a named trusted person is the power to close accounts plus a 'catalog' of metadata — send/receive timestamps and sender or recipient details — while the actual contents of emails, private messages, videos, photos and attachments require the decedent to have expressly granted that authority to the personal representative fiduciary.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: The content-versus-catalog split is the single decision point that determines whether an estate can recover monetizable digital assets; drafting language, not technology, is the bottleneck.
insights.quote: grants the authority to the personal representative fiduciary,
insights.locator: Under RUFADAA, a named trusted person

insights.claim: The legal theory behind RUFADAA is that digital property differs from tangible property because a fiduciary receiving forwarded mail gets only incoming communications, whereas email access hands over a searchable history the deceased may have expected to stay private.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: A reusable mental model — flow versus archive — that explains why every platform will treat inherited access to historical data more restrictively than access to new activity.
insights.quote: At the heart of RUFADAA is this recognition that digital property is in some ways different from traditional, tangible property,

insights.claim: Cryptocurrency held in a private wallet whose key nobody else has is permanently unrecoverable at death, whereas crypto held by a third party such as Coinbase or PayPal can be passed on through the estate process.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Inheritance friction is a structural, demographic tailwind for custodial exchanges and a permanent supply-destruction mechanism for self-custodied coins — relevant both to exchange revenue and to circulating-supply models.
insights.quote: If it's stored in a private wallet and no one has the key, the money is lost forever.

insights.claim: Social media accounts that earn dividends create an unresolved question of how a beneficiary collects future proceeds and whether the account should be kept alive at all, making creator accounts a cash-flowing asset with no established succession mechanism.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: As the creator economy ages, monetized-account succession becomes a real asset class problem — watch for platforms or specialists that build transferable creator-account rights.
insights.locator: Digital assets can have as much monetary value

themes.theme: Platform legacy tools override your will

insights.claim: A platform's own online legacy controls take top priority and can override the instructions a person writes into their will, which is why the recommended action is to name a fiduciary in a will and deliberately NOT enable the built-in legacy features.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: The advice inverts the intuitive default of using platform tools; it signals that private contract terms currently outrank probate documents, a governance gap regulators or standards bodies will eventually attack.
insights.quote: a platform’s own online controls take top priority and thus could override what you put into your instructions
insights.locator: Also, do not enable those legacy features

insights.claim: Google has offered Inactive Account Manager since 2013 and Apple and Meta use 'legacy contact' terminology, with Instagram filing the same function under 'memorialization' — inconsistent naming across custodians that itself obstructs users finding the feature.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Thirteen-plus years after Google shipped the first tool the category still has no common vocabulary — evidence that no incumbent is investing here and that the standards gap is wide open.

insights.claim: Instagram's death-transfer flow requires the designated recipient to already hold an Instagram account before they can download a decedent's content, embedding user acquisition into the bereavement process.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: A concrete example of platforms designing inheritance to retain users rather than to serve estates — the kind of dark-pattern detail that draws consumer-protection scrutiny.
insights.locator: For example, if you want to give someone permission

insights.claim: There is no defined technical or procedural way to tell an online provider that a user has died or lost capacity, so every built-in legacy tool still depends on a human successfully reaching the company by unspecified means.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
entities: Death in the Digital Estate Community Group
insights.so_what: This is the identity-infrastructure hole that makes all downstream tooling brittle; whoever standardizes the death/incapacity signal captures a chokepoint across every consumer platform.
insights.quote: there is no defined way to tell a provider that someone has died or lost capacity.

insights.claim: The OpenID Foundation has stood up a Death in the Digital Estate Community Group whose long-term goal is developing protocols and guidance for users to manage their digital estates.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: A standards effort at this early a stage is the leading indicator to track for when identity vendors and password managers get an interoperable hook to build against.
insights.locator: His group has the long-term goal

insights.claim: Users who never gave a platform their real name or real date of birth leave their trusted contact unable to prove the account was ever theirs, converting past privacy hygiene into an inheritance failure mode.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Pseudonymity and estate recoverability are directly in tension — a design constraint any privacy-first identity product will eventually have to price in.
insights.locator: What happens if you never gave your real name

themes.theme: Why DIY handoffs fail in practice

insights.claim: Biometric-gated two-factor authentication apps defeat credential handoff entirely: even a trusted person holding every password from a password manager cannot complete logins that require the decedent's fingerprint.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Security hardening and estate recoverability move in opposite directions — a real product gap for password managers and MFA vendors to solve with recovery delegation.
insights.quote: my two-factor authentication app is protected by biometrics

insights.claim: A colleague of an OpenID Foundation working-group co-chair built a DIY digital-estate handoff system, then tested it from his trusted person's perspective and failed at the very first step, indicating even expert-designed solutions break on first contact.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Treat any digital-estate solution as unvalidated until dry-run tested from the successor's seat; the failure rate among sophisticated users is the market opportunity.
insights.locator: Kiser says that one of his colleagues

insights.claim: Someone other than the account holder logging in with inherited credentials likely violates the data custodian's terms of service, and enforcement is plausible in high-profile cases such as celebrities and public figures.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Credential-sharing workarounds carry legal tail risk, which is why the durable solution has to be contractual and statutory rather than technical.

insights.claim: Credentials must never be listed in a will because a will is a public document; the will should name the person and the specific assets, while passwords are shared separately and only with the people who need them.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: A hard operational rule that splits the legal instrument from the secret store — and explains why password managers with legacy features sit adjacent to, not inside, the legal workflow.
insights.quote: the will is a public document.
insights.locator: The way to give that permission

insights.claim: An unencrypted USB drive holding a full local export of your data is a workable fallback for heirs but requires disciplined regular re-export and still does nothing to terminate the online accounts you want closed.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Data preservation and account termination are two separate problems; solutions that solve only one leave a recurring liability behind.
insights.locator: One other possibility is to create a local backup

insights.claim: The single most important maintenance step is updating final-instruction documents every time accounts change or assets move, meaning digital estate planning is a recurring obligation rather than a one-time filing.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Recurring-maintenance framing is what turns digital estate planning into a subscription business rather than a one-off legal fee.
insights.locator: Most important of all, update your final instructions

insights.claim: Even where wishes are written into a will, family in-fighting over a decedent's accounts remains the likeliest real-world outcome — the will's practical value is the legal protection it gives the fiduciary rather than conflict avoidance.
insights.speaker: Jill Duffy
insights.so_what: Sets realistic expectations for what estate documentation buys — indemnity, not harmony — which is how such services should actually be underwritten and sold.
insights.locator: A more likely scenario is that loved ones disagree
